title: Piano Concerto in G major
hook: A whip crack, a Basque tune, a touch of jazz, and a slow melody that Ravel said nearly killed him.

painting.title: Basque Celebration (Dance at El Antiguo, San Sebastián)
painting.collection: Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya, Barcelona
painting.pairingNote: Women dance on a grassy headland above San Sebastián bay while a pipe and drum play, on the Basque coast just across the border from Ravel’s birthplace; the concerto’s opening tune has a Basque lilt.

facts: Ravel wrote the concerto between 1929 and 1931, at the same time as his Concerto for the Left Hand for the pianist Paul Wittgenstein. It was his second-to-last work.

He said he wanted a real concerto, brilliant and showing off the soloist, without trying to be profound, and that his models were Mozart and Saint-Saëns. Two other influences can be heard: jazz, which he had enjoyed in Paris and on his American tour of 1928, and the Basque music of his mother’s country. He was born in Ciboure, a Basque town on the French coast.

He meant to play the solo part himself, but poor health made him hand it to Marguerite Long, to whom it is dedicated. She gave the first performance on 14 January 1932 at the Salle Pleyel in Paris, with Ravel conducting the Lamoureux Orchestra. Within days they set off on a tour of sixteen European cities.
The orchestra is small, almost a chamber orchestra, with one each of most wind instruments and a busy percussion section, including a whip.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a whip crack, a festival and the blues (I), a long, calm song (II), a mad dash with the same four chords at each end (III).

movements.heading: Allegramente
movements.summary: A crack of the whip, and a piccolo whistles a perky tune over the piano’s glittering patterns. The movement brings together five themes: the first suggests a Basque folk tune, the second Spain, and the others the blues and jazz. Where a single [[cadenza|cadenza]] might be expected, Ravel writes three: first for the harp, then for the woodwinds, and finally for the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The festival tune
mainIdeas.description: a perky melody for piccolo, then trumpet, over rippling piano patterns in two keys at once.

mainIdeas.name: The blues
mainIdeas.description: a slow, swaying melody with “blue” notes, first sung by the piano alone.

mainIdeas.name: The jazz trumpet
mainIdeas.description: a brassy, bending tune that sounds like a dance band.

stops.hear: A whip crack; the piccolo whistles a tune while the piano glitters underneath; the trumpet takes it up
stops.happening: The first theme. The piano plays in two keys at once, a touch of [[bitonality|bitonality]]

stops.hear: Sharper, Spanish-sounding rhythms in the orchestra and piano
The music slows; the piano alone plays a swaying, bluesy melody
A muted trumpet and the woodwinds play a sly, jazzy tune; the piano joins in
stops.happening: More jazz themes. The end of the [[exposition|exposition]]

stops.hear: The opening bustle returns, now racing and full of brilliant piano runs
The whip and the piccolo tune again
The harp plays alone, then woodwinds take turns with the blues tune
stops.happening: The first two “cadenzas”, for harp and for woodwinds

stops.hear: The piano alone sings the blues melody, high, over long, shimmering [[trill|trill]]s

stops.label: Last 90 seconds
stops.hear: Fast again: the orchestra rushes in, and the movement ends with a cascade of falling chords

notice: In the piano cadenza, listen to the right hand. It plays the melody and a trill at the same time.
Notice the jazz colours: muted trumpet, sliding notes, the “blue” notes that slip between major and minor.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Martha Argerich recorded the concerto in Berlin in 1967, with Claudio Abbado and the Berlin Philharmonic; both were early in their careers. On the Spotify album the concerto is tracks 4–6, after Prokofiev’s Third Concerto, which was its partner on the original LP.

movements.heading: Adagio assai
movements.summary: After the fun of the first movement, stillness. The piano plays alone for about three minutes: one long, calm melody that never repeats itself, over a steady, gently swaying accompaniment. Ravel took the slow movement of Mozart’s Clarinet Quintet as his model, and said the melody nearly killed him. Then the orchestra enters, the music clouds over for a while, and the cor anglais brings back the melody while the piano decorates it.

mainIdeas.name: The melody
mainIdeas.description: a long, unbroken line in the right hand, slow and calm, like a stately dance.

mainIdeas.name: The accompaniment
mainIdeas.description: a steady swaying in the left hand that seems to pull against the melody’s beat.

stops.hear: The piano alone: a slow, swaying accompaniment and a long, calm melody above it
stops.happening: The main melody, in E major

stops.hear: A flute enters softly, then oboe and clarinet carry the music onwards
stops.happening: The orchestra joins; the second idea

stops.hear: The harmony grows more clouded; slowly rising chords in the orchestra, sparkling patterns in the piano
The cor anglais plays the opening melody, while the piano weaves delicate patterns high above
stops.happening: The melody returns, in a new colour

stops.label: Last minute
stops.hear: The piano’s last [[trill|trill]]s and soft chords; the music fades
stops.happening: A quiet close in E major

notice: When the cor anglais returns with the melody, the piano is no longer the singer. Listen to it decorating instead, high and light.

movements.heading: Presto
movements.summary: The shortest movement and the wildest. Four sharp chords launch a whirlwind of fast notes for the piano, with shrieking clarinets and piccolo, brassy fanfares and a trombone that seems to bray like a donkey. Some hear the circus or a fairground. The same four chords end it.

mainIdeas.name: The four chords
mainIdeas.description: a sharp signal from the orchestra, heard at the start and the end.

mainIdeas.name: The toccata
mainIdeas.description: rapid, quiet notes running through the piano part from start to finish.

stops.hear: Four loud, sharp chords; the piano sets off at full speed with soft, rapid notes
stops.happening: The opening signal and the main theme

stops.hear: Shrill clarinets and piccolo; a trombone slides comically
stops.happening: The carnival colours of the orchestra, with a trombone [[glissando|glissando]]

stops.hear: Brassy fanfares and a jaunty, march-like tune
stops.happening: A new theme in the brass and woodwinds

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A final rush, then the same four chords
stops.happening: The movement ends as it began

notice: The piano almost never stops in this movement. Listen to how soft its rapid notes can be, even at this speed.

threads.title: Fun first
threads.body: Ravel said he wanted to entertain, like Mozart, rather than to be profound. Only the slow movement breaks the spell.

threads.title: Jazz and Basque
threads.body: Blues and dance-band colours sit beside a Basque-flavoured opening, a mix that is all Ravel’s own.

threads.title: A small orchestra
threads.body: With one of each wind instrument and a whip, the orchestra plays like a band of soloists, and every colour stands out.
